name: Python Core Fundamentals
description: 48 questions on Python gotchas, memory, built-ins, scope, typing, the object model, and concurrency. Assume Python 3.11+ unless stated; GIL questions explicitly distinguish CPython builds. Topic selection includes an anecdotal [candidate report](https://leetcode.com/discuss/post/7303754/), not a statistical frequency ranking. Answers reference primary documentation. No SQL or Django patterns.

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items

a = add(1)
b = add(2)
print(a, a is b)
```
questions.explanation: The default list is created once when `def` executes. Both calls return that same list; the second call also changes what `a` references. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
def change(items):
    items.append(2)
    items = [9]

a = [1]
change(a)
print(a)
```
questions.explanation: Arguments bind local names to objects. Mutation affects the shared list; rebinding the local name does not rebind `a` in the caller. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(3)
b.append([4])
print(a)
```
questions.explanation: The outer lists are independent, but the shallow copy shares their existing inner lists. Appending to `b` itself does not change `a`. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/copy.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
rows = [[0] * 2] * 3
rows[0][1] = 7
print(rows)
```
questions.explanation: Repetition reuses references to one inner list. Use a comprehension to construct a separate list for each row. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html).

questions.question: Which comparisons are appropriate for the stated purpose?
options: `left == right` to compare built-in string contents
`left is right` to compare integer values independently of object caching
`left is right` to test whether two names reference the same object
answers: `left == right` to compare built-in string contents
`left is right` to test whether two names reference the same object
questions.explanation: Identity and equality answer different questions. Interning or integer caching does not make `is` a portable value-comparison operator. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html).

questions.question:
After the exception is caught, what is printed?

```python
t = ([1],)
try:
    t[0] += [2]
except TypeError:
    pass
print(t)
```
questions.explanation: The list is extended before Python attempts to assign it back into the tuple slot. That assignment fails, but the mutation remains. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
d = {True: "a", 1: "b", 1.0: "c"}
print(len(d), d[True])
```
questions.explanation: These numeric keys compare equal and have equal hashes, so they address one dictionary entry. Each assignment replaces its value. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html).

questions.question: Given `a = [1]` and `b = a`, executing `del a` removes the name `a` but leaves the list reachable through `b`.
questions.explanation: `del a` removes `a` binding. The list remains reachable through `b`; deletion of `a` name is not destruction of its object. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html).

questions.question: In ordinary GIL-enabled CPython, why is cyclic garbage collection needed in addition to reference counting?
options: It frees all objects immediately after each function returns
It copies live objects into new local variables
It prevents Python code from creating reference cycles
Unreachable objects can keep each other’s reference counts above zero
questions.answer: Unreachable objects can keep each other’s reference counts above zero
questions.explanation: Reference counting alone cannot reclaim an unreachable cycle whose members still reference one another. Cyclic collection complements it. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html).

questions.question: A timeout of 0 is valid; only `None` should select the default 30. Which expression meets that requirement?
options: `30 if timeout is None else timeout`
questions.answer: `30 if timeout is None else timeout`
questions.explanation: `or` selects its fallback for any falsy value, including zero. An explicit `None` check preserves other valid values. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
values = [3, 1, 2]
result = values.sort()
print(values, result)
```
questions.explanation: `list.sort` changes the list in place and returns `None`. `sorted(values)` instead returns a new sorted list. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html).

questions.question: What happens when `list(zip([1, 2], ["a"], strict=True))` is evaluated?
options: It pads the second pair with `None`
It raises `TypeError` because strict is unsupported in Python 3.11
questions.explanation: `strict=True` detects unequal lengths instead of silently truncating. `zip` is lazy, so consumption triggers the mismatch error. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html).

questions.question: What is the value of `(all([]), any([]))`?
questions.explanation: No element violates `all` on an empty iterable, while no element satisfies `any`. Both functions also short-circuit on decisive elements. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
d = dict.fromkeys(["a", "b"], [])
d["a"].append(1)
print(d["b"])
```
questions.explanation: `fromkeys` uses the same supplied value for every key. A dictionary comprehension can create independent lists. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html).

questions.question:
What happens when `f()` is called?

```python
x = 10
def f():
    print(x)
    x = 20
```
options: It prints 10 and changes the global `x`
It prints 10 and creates a local `x`
questions.explanation: Assignment makes `x` local throughout this function. The preceding read therefore accesses an unbound local rather than the global `x`. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html).

questions.question: An inner function must rebind an existing `counter` in its enclosing function, without changing a module global. Which declaration is appropriate?
questions.explanation: `nonlocal` targets an existing binding in an enclosing function scope. Mutation of an already-referenced object is different from rebinding a name. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/executionmodel.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs], [f() for f in fixed])
```
questions.explanation: The closures look up a shared variable when called. Default arguments capture each current integer when the corresponding lambda is created. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html).

questions.question:
What is printed in Python 3?

```python
x = 99
values = [x for x in range(3)]
print(x, values)
```
questions.explanation: A comprehension’s iteration variable does not overwrite the surrounding binding. A normal `for` statement has different scope behavior. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html).

questions.question:
Given this function, which calls are valid?

```python
def f(a, /, b, *, c):
    return a + b + c
```
questions.explanation: `a` is positional-only, `b` accepts either form, and `c` is keyword-only. All three remain required. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html).

questions.question:
What happens?

```python
def f(x, **kwargs):
    return x, kwargs

f(1, **{"x": 2})
```
questions.explanation: The call supplies `x` both positionally and by keyword. `**kwargs` does not absorb a duplicate assignment to an existing named parameter. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
it = iter([1, 2])
print(list(it), list(it))
```
questions.explanation: An iterator carries traversal state. The first `list` call consumes it; calling `iter` on the original `list` would create a fresh iterator. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/functional.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
def values():
    print("start")
    yield 1

g = values()
print("created")
print(next(g))
```
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function creates the generator without running its body. `next` begins execution and pauses at `yield`. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/functional.html).

questions.question:
What is `list(outer())`?

```python
def inner():
    yield 1
    return 7

def outer():
    result = yield from inner()
    yield result
```
questions.explanation: `yield from` forwards yielded items and evaluates to the subgenerator’s return value when that generator finishes. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html).
Decorators are applied from the bottom upward: `b` wraps the original function, then `a` wraps that result. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html).

questions.question: What does `functools.wraps` normally provide for a decorator wrapper?
options: Preservation of metadata such as `__name__` and `__doc__`
Automatic enforcement of the original parameter types
Automatic conversion of a synchronous wrapper into an async function
answers: Preservation of metadata such as `__name__` and `__doc__`
questions.explanation: `wraps` updates wrapper metadata. It does not implement argument validation or change the wrapper’s execution model. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html).

questions.question: A context manager’s `__enter__` succeeds. Its block raises `ValueError`, and `__exit__` returns `True`. What happens?
options: The exception is suppressed and execution continues after `with`
The return value from `__exit__` replaces the `with`-bound variable
questions.answer: The exception is suppressed and execution continues after `with`
questions.explanation: A truthy `__exit__` result suppresses the block’s exception. The `with`-bound value instead comes from `__enter__`. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html).

questions.question: A generator decorated with `contextlib.contextmanager` acquires a resource before `yield`. Where should its unconditional cleanup usually go?
options: In the caller’s garbage collector callback
questions.explanation: Exceptions from the `with` body are injected at `yield`. A surrounding `finally` handles both normal completion and exceptional exit. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextlib.html).

questions.question:
What does `f()` do in Python 3.11–3.14 with default warning handling?

```python
def f():
    try:
        raise ValueError("bad")
    finally:
        return 2
```
questions.explanation: A `return` leaving `finally` overrides pending control flow, including an exception. CPython 3.14 also emits a `SyntaxWarning` for this pattern when compiling the function; with default warning handling, calling it still returns `2`. Avoid this pattern because it hides failures. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#finally-clause).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
class Bag:
    items = []

a = Bag()
b = Bag()
a.items.append(1)
b.items = [2]
print(a.items, b.items, Bag.items)
```
questions.explanation: The append mutates the shared class list. Assignment to `b.items` creates an instance attribute that shadows that class attribute. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html).

questions.question: In cooperative multiple inheritance, what does `super().method()` use to find the next implementation?
options: The first class declared anywhere in the module
The method resolution order for the relevant instance class
Only the direct base named first in the source file
questions.answer: The method resolution order for the relevant instance class
questions.explanation: `super` continues lookup through the MRO after the current class. Cooperative methods need compatible signatures and consistent `super` calls. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html).

questions.question: A plain class defines `__eq__` but does not define or explicitly inherit a usable `__hash__`. What is the usual effect on its instances?
options: They receive a constant hash automatically
They hash using the result of `__eq__`
questions.explanation: Python sets `__hash__` to `None` when equality is overridden without a hash implementation. Equal hashable objects must have equal hashes. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html).

questions.question: Which statements about dataclasses are correct?
options: `field(default_factory=list)` creates a fresh list for each instance using that default
`frozen=True` recursively freezes every object in every field
A list stored in a `frozen` dataclass can still be mutated
Ordinary dataclass annotations validate field values automatically at runtime
answers: `field(default_factory=list)` creates a fresh list for each instance using that default
A list stored in a `frozen` dataclass can still be mutated
questions.explanation: Factories avoid shared defaults. `frozen` restricts ordinary field assignment, not nested mutation; annotations alone do not validate constructor inputs. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html).

questions.question: Why can `obj.name` invoke getter logic when `name` is defined with `@property` on the class?
options: The getter runs only when parentheses are added
`property` implements the descriptor protocol used by attribute access
Every attribute read calls every class method
The `property` is replaced with a string when the class is created
questions.answer: `property` implements the descriptor protocol used by attribute access
questions.explanation: Properties are descriptors. Their protocol methods participate in attribute access, allowing managed reads and writes behind attribute syntax. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html).

questions.question:
Given this function, which statement is correct?

```python
def f(value: str | None):
    return value
```
options: `f(123)` is rejected automatically by Python’s ordinary annotation handling
`f()` raises `TypeError` because no default was supplied
The annotation prohibits an empty string
questions.answer: `f()` raises `TypeError` because no default was supplied
questions.explanation: Nullable and optional-to-pass are separate ideas. An annotation admitting `None` does not supply a default or enforce runtime validation. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html).

questions.question:
What is printed?

```python
from typing import cast
x = cast(int, "12")
print(type(x).__name__, x)
```
questions.explanation: `cast` returns its input unchanged. It tells a static checker how to treat the expression; it does not convert or validate the value. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html).

questions.question: A function expects a `typing.Protocol` whose only required member is a `send` method. How can another class satisfy it for static checking?
options: It must inherit from that `Protocol` directly
It must register with the garbage collector
It can provide `send` with a compatible signature without inheriting the `Protocol`
questions.answer: It can provide `send` with a compatible signature without inheriting the `Protocol`
questions.explanation: Protocols support structural subtyping. A matching interface can satisfy a protocol without nominal inheritance. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html).

questions.question: A `TypedDict` declaration describes dictionary keys and value types for static checking, but its runtime instances are ordinary dictionaries.
questions.explanation: `TypedDict` describes dictionary structure for static checkers. Its runtime instances are ordinary dictionaries; boundary validation requires additional code or tooling. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html).

questions.question: Which statements correctly distinguish GIL-enabled and free-threaded CPython?
options: In a GIL-enabled interpreter, ordinary Python bytecode is generally executed by one thread at a time
Blocking I/O can release the GIL, allowing useful thread concurrency
Every CPython 3.13+ installation always runs with the GIL disabled
A free-threaded build can run Python threads in parallel, subject to runtime and extension compatibility
answers: In a GIL-enabled interpreter, ordinary Python bytecode is generally executed by one thread at a time
Blocking I/O can release the GIL, allowing useful thread concurrency
A free-threaded build can run Python threads in parallel, subject to runtime and extension compatibility
questions.explanation: Build and runtime configuration matter. Free-threaded CPython exists; importing an incompatible extension can re-enable the GIL. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html).

questions.question: In GIL-enabled CPython, a multi-step check-then-update on shared application state is automatically a thread-safe transaction.
questions.explanation: The GIL is not an application lock. Multi-step invariants need synchronization even if some individual operations happen to be atomic. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html).

questions.question: Large independent CPU-heavy jobs spend almost all their time in pure Python code. Under GIL-enabled CPython, which approach most directly enables multicore execution?
options: A process pool, after accounting for serialization and startup costs
More asyncio tasks on one event-loop thread
Replacing each function with an `async def` but adding no awaits
A thread pool guaranteed to scale linearly with core count
questions.answer: A process pool, after accounting for serialization and startup costs
questions.explanation: Processes can execute Python work on separate cores. Native extensions that release the GIL can change the thread-versus-process trade-off. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html).

questions.question:
What does the assignment do by itself?

```python
async def work():
    return 7

coro = work()
```
options: Runs work to completion and binds 7
Creates a coroutine object without scheduling its body
questions.answer: Creates a coroutine object without scheduling its body
questions.explanation: Calling a coroutine function creates an object. Await it or schedule it to execute its body. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html).

questions.question:
Inside an async function, how do these statements behave when `first` and `second` are freshly called coroutine functions?

```python
await first()
await second()
```
options: `second` starts `first` because await reverses call order
They execute on separate CPU cores
questions.explanation: Direct awaits here are sequential. Creating both tasks before awaiting their results allows their waiting periods to overlap. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html).

questions.question: An `async` handler calls a synchronous blocking network client on its event-loop thread. What is the most direct problem?
options: `async def` automatically rejects synchronous function calls
The function’s return type becomes a `Task`
Other tasks on that event loop cannot progress while the call blocks
questions.answer: Other tasks on that event loop cannot progress while the call blocks
questions.explanation: Use an `async` client or suitable thread offloading for blocking I/O. Declaring the caller `async` does not transform synchronous callees. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-dev.html).

questions.question: Every `await` expression necessarily gives another asyncio task a turn, even if the awaited operation completes immediately.
questions.explanation: An awaitable may complete without suspending. Cooperative scheduling requires actual suspension; `asyncio.sleep(0)` explicitly offers a scheduling opportunity. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html).

questions.question: One child of `await asyncio.gather(a(), b())` raises `ValueError`. The caller catches it and keeps the event loop running. With default `return_exceptions=False`, what does `gather` itself do?
options: Propagates the exception promptly without automatically cancelling the other child
Waits for every child before raising the first exception
Cancels the other child before propagating
Returns the exception as a result element
questions.answer: Propagates the exception promptly without automatically cancelling the other child
questions.explanation: `gather` does not cancel siblings on an ordinary child failure. Runner shutdown or separate cancellation can still stop them later. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html).

questions.question: Inside an `asyncio.TaskGroup`, one child raises `ValueError` while others are pending. Assuming cooperative cancellation and no other failures, what happens when the group exits?
options: The error is silently stored in a result list
Other children are left running after exit
Remaining children are cancelled and awaited, then an `ExceptionGroup` is raised
Only the failing child is awaited
questions.answer: Remaining children are cancelled and awaited, then an `ExceptionGroup` is raised
questions.explanation: `TaskGroup` gives related tasks a shared lifetime. Ordinary child failures trigger sibling cancellation and grouped exception reporting. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html).

questions.question: Which practices correctly handle asyncio task cancellation?
options: Use `try/finally` for cleanup around cancellable work
If `CancelledError` is caught for cleanup, normally re-raise it
answers: Use `try/finally` for cleanup around cancellable work
If `CancelledError` is caught for cleanup, normally re-raise it
questions.explanation: `asyncio.CancelledError` inherits from `BaseException`. Cancellation is cooperative, and suppressing it can disrupt structured concurrency. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-exceptions.html).

questions.question:
Two tasks on one event loop both execute this sequence against the same shared `counter`. How should they protect the read-modify-write invariant?

```python
value = counter
await some_io()
counter = value + 1
```
options: No protection is needed because there is one thread
Use a shared `asyncio.Lock` around the critical sequence, or redesign to avoid the interleaving
Use separate locks created inside each task
questions.answer: Use a shared `asyncio.Lock` around the critical sequence, or redesign to avoid the interleaving
questions.explanation: Tasks can interleave at suspension points and overwrite each other’s updates. A shared asyncio lock coordinates tasks, not separate processes or threads. [Source](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-sync.html).
